{{Short description|Mathematical transformation}}
{{No footnotes|date=January 2025}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Stieltjes transformation''' {{math|''S''<sub>''ρ''</sub>(''z'')}} of a measure of density {{math|''ρ''}} on a real interval {{mvar|I}} is the function of the complex variable {{mvar|z}} defined outside {{mvar|I}} by the formula

<math display="block">S_{\rho}(z)=\int_I\frac{\rho(t)\,dt}{t-z}, \qquad z \in \mathbb{C} \setminus I.</math>

==Inverse formula==
Under certain conditions we can reconstitute the density function {{math|''ρ''}} starting from its Stieltjes transformation thanks to the inverse formula of Stieltjes–Perron.<!-- Check if this is [[Oskar Perron]]. --> For example, if the density {{math|''ρ''}} is continuous throughout {{mvar|I}}, one will have inside this interval
<math display="block">
  \rho(x) = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \frac{S_{\rho}(x+i\varepsilon)-S_{\rho}(x-i\varepsilon)}{2i\pi}.
</math>

===Derivation of formula===
Recall from basic calculus that
<math display="block">
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1}{x^2 + 1} dx =
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \arctan x - \lim_{x\to-\infty} \arctan x =
  \tfrac{\pi}{2} - (-\tfrac{\pi}{2}) = 
  \pi \text{.}
</math>
Hence <math> f(x) = \tfrac{1}{\pi} (x^2+1)^{-1} </math> is the probability density function of a distribution—a [[Cauchy distribution]]. Via the change of variables <math> x = (t - t_0) / \varepsilon </math> we get the full family of Cauchy distributions:
<math display="block">
  1 = 
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1/\pi}{ x^2 + 1 } dx =
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{1/\pi}{ (\frac{t-t_0}{\varepsilon})^2 + 1 } \frac{dx}{dt} dt =
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{ \varepsilon/\pi }{ (t-t_0)^2 + \varepsilon^2 } dt
</math>
As <math> \varepsilon \to 0^+ </math>, these tend to a [[Dirac distribution]] with the mass at <math> t_0 </math>. Integrating any function <math> \rho(t) </math> against ''that'' would pick out the value <math> \rho(t_0) </math>. Rather integrating
<math display="block">
  \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{ \varepsilon/\pi }{ (t-t_0)^2 + \varepsilon^2 } \rho(t) \, dt
</math>
for some <math> \varepsilon > 0 </math> instead produces the value at <math> t_0 </math> for some smoothed variant of <math> \rho </math>—the smaller the value of <math> \varepsilon </math>, the less smoothing is applied. Used in this way, the factor <math> \frac{ \varepsilon/\pi }{ (t-t_0)^2 + \varepsilon^2 } </math> is also known as the [[Poisson kernel]] (for the half-plane).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Colbrook |first1=Matthew J. |title=Computing Spectral Measures and Spectral Types |journal=Communications in Mathematical Physics |date=2021 |volume=384 |pages=433–501 |doi=10.1007/s00220-021-04072-4 |ref=Colbrook|arxiv=1908.06721 }}</ref>

The denominator <math> (t-t_0)^2 + \varepsilon^2 </math> has no real zeroes, but it has two complex zeroes <math> t = t_0 \pm i\varepsilon </math>, and thus there is a partial fraction decomposition
<math display="block">
  \frac{ \varepsilon/\pi }{ (t-t_0)^2 + \varepsilon^2 } =
  \frac{ 1/2\pi i }{ t - (t_0 + i\varepsilon) } - \frac{ 1/2\pi i }{ t - (t_0 - i\varepsilon) }
</math>
Hence for any measure <math> \mu </math>,
<math display="block">
  \int_\mathbb{R} \frac{ \varepsilon/\pi }{ (t-x)^2 + \varepsilon^2 } d\mu(t) =
  \frac{1}{2 \pi i} \int_\mathbb{R} \left( \frac{1}{t - (x + i\varepsilon)} - \frac{1}{t - (x - i\varepsilon)} \right) d\mu(t) =
  \frac{ S_\mu(x + i\varepsilon) - S_\mu(x - i\varepsilon) }{ 2\pi i }
</math>
If the measure <math> \mu </math> is [[absolutely continuous]] (with respect to the Lebesgue measure) at <math> x </math> then as <math> \varepsilon \to 0^+ </math> that integral tends to the density at <math> x </math>. If instead the measure has a point mass at <math> x </math>, then the limit as <math> \varepsilon \to 0^+ </math> of the integral diverges, and the Stieltjes transform <math> S_\mu </math> has a pole at <math> x </math>.

==Connections with moments of measures==
{{Main|Moment problem}}

If the measure of density {{math|''ρ''}} has [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] of any order defined for each integer by the equality
<math display="block">m_{n}=\int_I t^n\,\rho(t)\,dt,</math>

then the [[Stieltjes]] transformation of {{math|''ρ''}} admits for each integer {{mvar|n}} the [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic]] expansion in the neighbourhood of infinity given by
<math display="block">S_{\rho}(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{m_k}{z^{k+1}}+o\left(\frac{1}{z^{n+1}}\right).</math>

Under certain conditions the complete expansion as a [[Laurent series]] can be obtained:
<math display="block">S_{\rho}(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{m_n}{z^{n+1}}.</math>

==Relationships to orthogonal polynomials==

The correspondence <math display="inline">(f,g) \mapsto \int_I f(t) g(t) \rho(t) \, dt</math>  defines an [[inner product]] on the space of [[continuous function]]s on the interval {{mvar|I}}.

If {{math|{''P<sub>n</sub>''}<nowiki/>}} is a sequence of [[orthogonal polynomials]] for this product, we can create the sequence of associated [[secondary polynomials]] by the formula
<math display="block">Q_n(x)=\int_I \frac{P_n (t)-P_n (x)}{t-x}\rho (t)\,dt.</math>

It appears that <math display="inline">F_n(z) = \frac{Q_n(z)}{P_n(z)}</math> is a [[Padé approximation]] of {{math|''S''<sub>''ρ''</sub>(''z'')}} in a neighbourhood of infinity, in the sense that
<math display="block">S_\rho(z)-\frac{Q_n(z)}{P_n(z)}=O\left(\frac{1}{z^{2n+1}}\right).</math>

Since these two sequences of polynomials satisfy the same recurrence relation in three terms, we can develop a [[generalized continued fraction|continued fraction]] for the Stieltjes transformation whose successive [[Convergent (continued fraction)|convergents]] are the fractions {{math|''F<sub>n</sub>''(''z'')}}.

The Stieltjes transformation can also be used to construct from the density {{math|''ρ''}} an effective measure for transforming the secondary polynomials into an orthogonal system. (For more details see the article [[secondary measure]].)
